blocks.text: The full title is *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, in Chinese 《瑜伽師地論》, "Treatise on the Stages of the Yoga Practitioner". Ru-Yi's English title is *Treatise on the Stages of Yogic Practice*. Each part of the name is worth a moment.

items: **Yoga** (瑜伽) is explained by the Chinese commentators as **相應**, "correspondence" or "being joined in accord". The traditional commentaries list several kinds: accord with the object of contemplation, with practice, with fruition, with reason, and with the teaching. In the broadest sense, *yoga* is any practice in which body, speech, and mind are brought into accord with the truth.
**Ācāra** (行, "practice") makes *yogācāra*, "one who practises yoga", rendered 瑜伽師, "yoga master" or "yoga practitioner".

**Bhūmi** (地) means "ground" or "stage". The commentaries explain it as the ground that produces, sustains, and supports, like the earth, and also as the "domain" or "sphere" in which a practitioner moves.
**Śāstra** (論) is a treatise: a work that settles the nature and characteristics of dharmas by question and answer.

blocks.text: So the title promises a complete survey of the "grounds" on which a yoga practitioner stands and travels, from ordinary sense experience to final nirvāṇa. The treatise answers its own first question in just these terms: "What are the stages of the yoga practitioner? They are the seventeen stages." We shall read that line together on Day 1.

In the Chinese tradition the text is said to be "spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva" (彌勒菩薩說), and that is the byline in the Taishō edition we are reading. Xuánzàng's *Record of the Western Regions* (《大唐西域記》) preserves the story as it was told in India: at Ayodhyā, Asaṅga ascended at night to the Tuṣita heaven, received the *Yogācārabhūmi* and other works from Maitreya, and by day taught them to an assembly below.

The Tibetan tradition attributes the same text to **Asaṅga** (無著) as author. Modern scholars, studying the surviving Sanskrit and the different layers of the text, generally regard it as a compilation made over some time within a community of meditators, with parts such as the *Śrāvakabhūmi* (〈聲聞地〉) among its oldest material, and with Asaṅga as the figure most closely associated with its final form.

These views need not be set against each other in our reading. The Chinese teachers whose lectures we follow, Venerable Miào Jìng (妙境長老) and Master Cháng Bǎi (常柏法師), read the work as Maitreya's teaching recorded by Asaṅga, and they treat it as an authoritative map of the path. What matters for us is the map.
The treatise has one hundred fascicles (卷, *juan*, a "scroll" of roughly 7,000 to 10,000 characters), arranged in **five divisions** (五分):

items: **The Basic Section** (本地分, fascicles 1–50). It sets out the seventeen stages in order. Everything else in the treatise depends on it, as plants depend on the ground; hence "basic" or "root" (本).

**The Compendium of Ascertainments** (攝決擇分, fascicles 51–80). It returns to the seventeen stages and settles their deeper and more difficult points. Here the ālayavijñāna is argued for most fully, and here almost the whole *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* is quoted (fascicles 75–78).
**The Compendium of Explanations** (攝釋分, fascicles 81–82). It explains the method for expounding sūtras.
**The Compendium of Synonyms** (攝異門分, fascicles 83–84). It gathers the many names that the sūtras use for the same dharmas.
**The Compendium of Topics** (攝事分, fascicles 85–100). It summarises the essential subjects of the three collections of scripture, with much material parallel to the Āgamas.

blocks.text: The four later divisions all begin with 攝, "gathering" or "compendium": each gathers up and explains the Basic Section from a different angle.

The heart of the Basic Section is its list of **seventeen stages** (十七地), given first in a mnemonic verse, an **uddāna** (嗢拕南), and then in prose. Master Cháng Bǎi points out that the verse packs all seventeen into forty Chinese characters, and recommends this as a method of study: compress a passage into a few key words, and the whole will come back when needed. The seventeen are:

items: The stage corresponding to the five sense consciousnesses (五識身相應地)
The mind stage (意地)
The stage with initial and sustained thought (有尋有伺地)
The stage without initial but with sustained thought (無尋唯伺地)
The stage with neither (無尋無伺地)
The stage of meditative absorption (三摩呬多地)
The stage not of meditative absorption (非三摩呬多地)
The stage with mind (有心地)
The stage without mind (無心地)
The stage of wisdom arising from hearing (聞所成地)
The stage of wisdom arising from reflection (思所成地)
The stage of wisdom arising from cultivation (修所成地)
The stage of the hearers (聲聞地, *śrāvaka*)
The stage of the solitary realisers (獨覺地, *pratyekabuddha*)
The stage of the bodhisattvas (菩薩地)
The stage of nirvāṇa with remainder (有餘依地)
The stage of nirvāṇa without remainder (無餘依地)

blocks.text: Kuījī's commentary (《瑜伽師地論略纂》) groups them in three: stages 1–9 describe the **domain** (境) in which practice takes place, that is, the mind and its world; stages 10–15 describe **practice** (行); and stages 16–17 describe its **fruit** (果). The order is itself a teaching. One cannot transform the mind without first knowing how it works, and one cannot know how it works without starting from the most ordinary thing there is: a moment of seeing, hearing, or touching. That is why the whole hundred-fascicle work opens with the eye-consciousness.

secs.head: The treatise and the other Yogācāra texts

blocks.text: The *Yogācārabhūmi* is the root of a family of texts. Chinese tradition speaks of "**one root and ten branches**" (一本十支): this treatise is the root, and ten shorter treatises, among them the *Hundred Dharmas* (《百法明門論》), the *Five Aggregates* (《五蘊論》), the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (《攝大乘論》), the *Madhyāntavibhāga* (《辯中邊論》), and Vasubandhu's *Twenty* and *Thirty Verses*, are its branches. Several of these you have met already.
Four relationships are especially worth knowing.

items: **The Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra** (《解深密經》) is the scripture on which the school rests. The *Yogācārabhūmi* quotes nearly all of it in the *Compendium of Ascertainments*, so in a sense the sūtra lives inside the treatise.

**The Mahāyānasaṃgraha** (《攝大乘論》), by Asaṅga, organises Mahāyāna teaching around ten topics, beginning with the ālayavijñāna as "the support of what is to be known" (所知依). It is a systematic digest of ideas that the *Yogācārabhūmi* presents more diffusely.

**Vasubandhu's Thirty Verses** (《唯識三十頌》) condense the whole system into thirty stanzas, which the **Cheng Weishi Lun** (《成唯識論》), compiled by Xuánzàng in 659 from ten Indian commentaries, mainly following Dharmapāla, unfolds in great detail. The *Cheng Weishi Lun* became the standard textbook of the Chinese school, and our two teachers cite it constantly when explaining the *Yogācārabhūmi*.

**The Hundred Dharmas** (《百法明門論》) gives the list of a hundred dharmas in five groups: mind, mental factors, form, formations dissociated from mind, and the unconditioned. Its vocabulary underlies our Glossary.

blocks.text: Parts of the treatise were known in China before Xuánzàng. Dharmakṣema translated a version of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* as 《菩薩地持經》 in the early fifth century, and Guṇavarman produced another (《菩薩善戒經》); Paramārtha (真諦) translated a portion of the *Compendium of Ascertainments* (《決定藏論》). These partial versions raised more questions than they answered, and differences between Chinese teachers on the nature of mind, especially between followers of the *Daśabhūmika* commentary and of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, were a major reason why the young Xuánzàng resolved to go to India. His biography says he wished to obtain the *Seventeen Stages Treatise* (《十七地論》), that is, this work, in full.

At Nālandā he studied it with Śīlabhadra, then over a hundred years old, who is said to have been waiting for him. On his return Xuánzàng translated the complete text at the Hongfu Monastery (弘福寺) in Chang'an, between 646 and 648, in one hundred fascicles. Emperor Taizong wrote a preface for it, and a postface by the official Xǔ Jìngzōng (許敬宗) is printed at the end of fascicle 1 in the Taishō edition. That postface is not part of the treatise, so our daily readings leave it out.

Large parts of the Sanskrit original survive, including the first stages and the *Śrāvakabhūmi* and *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, and there is a complete Tibetan translation. For us, though, the Chinese of Xuánzàng is the primary text. It is careful, consistent in its terminology, and supported by fourteen centuries of Chinese commentary.
Each day's reading has the same parts:

items: **The text.** On the left (or above, on a phone), Xuánzàng's Chinese, taken unchanged from CBETA (T30, no. 1579), with the Taishō page, column, and line (for example 0279a22) at the start of each passage. On the right (or below), Ru-Yi's English translation, taken word for word, with spelling adjusted to British usage. Where Ru-Yi's translation has not yet rendered a passage, the handout says so plainly; it does not fill the gap with a new translation.

**The commentary.** These are our own English notes, written from the lectures of Venerable Miào Jìng (fascicles 1–50) and Master Cháng Bǎi (fascicles 1–100). Master Cháng Bǎi's lectures also draw on the layman Hán Qīngjìng's *Pīxún jì* (韓清淨《瑜伽師地論科句披尋記》), the modern outline-and-notes edition of the treatise.
**Key terms** and a few **check-yourself** questions, mostly from the Ru-Yi question bank.

blocks.text: Day 1 begins at the very beginning: "What are the stages of the yoga practitioner?"

quiz.q: How do the Chinese commentators explain the word "yoga" (瑜伽)?
options: As "correspondence" or "being joined in accord" (相應)
quiz.why: The commentaries gloss *yoga* as 相應, "correspondence": being joined in accord with the object, with practice, with fruition, with reason, and with the teaching.

quiz.q: Which division of the treatise sets out the seventeen stages and serves as the basis for the other four?
options: The Compendium of Ascertainments (攝決擇分)
quiz.why: The Basic Section, fascicles 1–50, is the "root" (本) on which the four "compendia" (攝…分) depend.

quiz.q: In Kuījī's grouping, stages 10–15 (hearing, reflection, cultivation, hearers, solitary realisers, bodhisattvas) describe what?
quiz.why: Stages 1–9 describe the domain, stages 10–15 describe practice, and stages 16–17 (nirvāṇa with and without remainder) describe the fruit.

quiz.q: Which sūtra is quoted almost entirely within the *Compendium of Ascertainments*?
quiz.why: Fascicles 75–78 quote nearly the whole *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* (《解深密經》), the chief scripture of the school.

quiz.q: Why do our daily readings leave out Xǔ Jìngzōng's text at the end of fascicle 1?
options: It is a postface to Xuánzàng's translation, not part of the treatise.
Ru-Yi has not translated it yet.
quiz.why: Xǔ Jìngzōng's postface (後序), printed after fascicle 1 in the Taishō edition, records the circumstances of the translation; it is not part of the treatise itself.
